questions.question: Q1. In the context of 4D printing, what does the fourth dimension represent?

answers.b: Time - the material transforms over time in response to stimuli.

explanations.a: Incorrect — We work in 3D space; time is the fourth dimension.
explanations.b: Correct — 4D printing adds time as a dimension; the object changes shape after printing when triggered.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Density is not related to the '4D' concept.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Cost does not define 4D printing.

questions.question: Q2. What are netpoints in a Shape Memory Polymer?

answers.a: Permanent crosslinks that store the memory of the original shape.
answers.b: Temporary connection points that form during heating.
answers.c: Regions where the material cracks under stress.
answers.d: Points where water molecules attach to the polymer.

explanations.a: Correct — Netpoints are permanent crosslinks (chemical or physical) that define the permanent shape.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Netpoints are permanent, not temporary.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Netpoints are not fracture sites.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Netpoints are mechanical features, not water-binding sites.

questions.question: Q3. The glass transition temperature (T_g) marks the boundary between which two states of a polymer?

explanations.a: Incorrect — T_g is not a vaporization transition.
explanations.b: Incorrect — T_g applies to amorphous polymers; it is not about crystallinity.
explanations.c: Correct — Below T_g the polymer is a stiff glass; above it the switching segments soften and it becomes rubbery.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The polymer remains solid at T_g; it undergoes a stiffness transition, not a phase change.

questions.question: Q4. What does the strain fixity ratio (R_f) quantify?

answers.a: The speed at which the material recovers its original shape.
answers.b: The fraction of applied strain that remains locked after unloading during programming.
answers.c: How easily the material breaks under tension.
answers.d: The maximum temperature the material can withstand.

explanations.a: Incorrect — This describes recovery rate, not strain fixity.
explanations.b: Correct — R_f is the percentage of loading strain that stays permanently fixed after the temporary shape is programmed and unloaded.
explanations.c: Incorrect — This relates to tensile strength.
explanations.d: Incorrect — This is thermal stability, not fixity.

questions.question: Q5. The Williams-Landel-Ferry (WLF) equation predicts how which property changes with temperature?

answers.c: The brittleness of the polymer below T_g.
answers.d: The relaxation time and viscosity shift above T_g.

explanations.a: Incorrect — WLF does not govern density changes.
explanations.b: Incorrect — WLF is not about optical properties.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Below T_g the relaxation time is effectively infinite; WLF applies above T_g.
explanations.d: Correct — The WLF equation gives the shift factor a_T, which scales how much faster the material relaxes as temperature rises above T_g.

questions.question: Q6. During shape recovery, what force drives the polymer back to its original permanent shape?

answers.a: The entropic restoring force supplied by the netpoints.

explanations.a: Correct — Once reheated above T_g, the netpoints exert an entropic spring-back that pulls the polymer toward its permanent shape.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Gravity is not the driver at the molecular scale.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Recovery is an internal process once heat unfreezes the switching segments.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Friction between chains resists motion rather than driving it.

questions.question: Q7. Which of the three model materials in this lab has the lowest glass transition temperature?

answers.d: All three have the same T_g.

explanations.a: Incorrect — PMMA has the highest T_g.
explanations.c: Correct — PU-SMP has T_g = 45°C, making it the easiest to trigger with modest heat.
explanations.d: Incorrect — The three materials have distinct T_g values.

questions.question: Q8. What is the primary objective of the programming step in Shape Memory Polymers?

answers.b: To increase the density of the material.
answers.c: To remove all the permanent shape memory.
answers.d: To write the temporary shape by loading the rubbery material, cooling it below T_g while stressed, then unloading.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Programming does not necessarily crystallize the material.
explanations.b: Incorrect — Programming does not significantly change density.
explanations.c: Incorrect — Programming preserves the netpoints and the permanent shape; it only adds a temporary shape.
explanations.d: Correct — Programming imprints a temporary shape by applying stress in the rubbery state, cooling to lock the strain, then releasing the load.

questions.question: Q9. Recovery kinetics in an SMP follows which mathematical law?

answers.b: First-order exponential decay toward the equilibrium strain.
answers.d: Constant rate independent of time and temperature.

explanations.a: Incorrect — Recovery slows exponentially, not linearly.
explanations.b: Correct — Strain recovery follows ε(t) = ε_eq + (ε_u - ε_eq)·exp(-t/τ), a first-order exponential decay.
explanations.c: Incorrect — The recovery rate depends exponentially on the relaxation time τ(T), not quadratically on T.
explanations.d: Incorrect — Recovery rate depends strongly on temperature and time.

questions.question: Q10. For biomedical applications at body temperature (37°C), which material offers the best activation temperature match?

answers.c: PMMA-SMP (T_g = 105°C) — far above body temperature for safety.
answers.d: None — all are too far from 37°C.

explanations.a: Correct — PU-SMP's T_g is within 10°C of 37°C, making it ideal for body-worn devices where ambient heat can nearly supply the trigger.
explanations.c: Incorrect — So high that body heat alone cannot trigger it.
explanations.d: Incorrect — PU-SMP is well-suited to biomedical use.
